q: Who invented the World Wide Web in 1989?
x: Berners-Lee worked at CERN and chose not to patent the Web, so anyone could build on it for free.

q: In which year was the first iPhone released to the public?
x: It went on sale on June 29, 2007, and people lined up for days outside stores.

q: What does RAM stand for in computing?
x: RAM holds the data your computer is using right now and is wiped when the power goes off.

q: What does LED stand for?
x: LEDs use far less energy than old incandescent bulbs and can last for tens of thousands of hours.

q: Which early graphical web browser, released in 1993, helped make the internet popular?
x: Mosaic was the first browser to show images inline with text, and its creators went on to build Netscape.

q: Which Swedish inventor created dynamite and left money in his will for annual prizes?
x: Nobel patented dynamite in 1867; his will created the Nobel Prizes, first awarded in 1901.

q: Which German engineer built the Patent-Motorwagen, often called the first practical automobile, in 1885?
x: His wife Bertha Benz made the first long-distance car trip in 1888 to prove the invention's worth.

q: What was the name of the first artificial satellite, launched in 1957?
x: Sputnik was about the size of a beach ball and beeped radio signals for three weeks.

q: The prefix 'tele-' in words like telephone and television means what?
x: It comes from Greek, and the same prefix appears in telescope, telegram, and telepathy.

q: A word spelled the same but pronounced differently, like 'lead' (to guide) and 'lead' (a metal), is called what?
x: English has many of these, such as 'tear' and 'wind'.

q: What is a phrase like 'deafening silence' or 'jumbo shrimp' called?
x: The word comes from Greek terms for 'sharp' and 'dull', which is itself an oxymoron.

q: Which figure of speech compares two things using 'like' or 'as'?
x: A metaphor makes the same kind of comparison but without using 'like' or 'as'.

q: Which language has the most native speakers in the world?
x: English has the most total speakers when second-language speakers are counted, but Mandarin leads for native speakers.

q: What is the study of the origin and history of words called?
x: Entomology, which sounds similar, is the study of insects.

q: The word 'alphabet' is built from the first two letters of which language's alphabet?
x: The Greek letters alpha and beta were themselves borrowed from Phoenician letters meaning 'ox' and 'house'.

q: What is the fear of heights called?
x: Acrophobia comes from the Greek word 'akron', meaning 'peak' or 'edge'.

q: Which Japanese word, meaning 'empty orchestra', names the pastime of singing along to backing tracks?
x: Karaoke was popularized in Japan in the 1970s and is now enjoyed worldwide.

q: Which Indian festival is known as the festival of colors?
x: Participants throw colored powder at each other to celebrate the arrival of spring.

q: On what date is Groundhog Day observed in North America?
x: According to tradition, if the groundhog sees its shadow, winter will last six more weeks.

q: On which date is Pi Day celebrated?
x: The date 3/14 matches the first digits of pi, 3.14, and the day is also Albert Einstein's birthday.

q: Black Friday, a major shopping day in the US, comes right after which holiday?
x: The name was used by Philadelphia police in the 1960s to describe the heavy traffic on that day.

q: What does IPO stand for in business?
x: An IPO is when a private company first sells shares to the public on a stock exchange.

q: What does GDP stand for in economics?
x: GDP measures the total value of goods and services a country produces in a given period.

q: What do economists call a general rise in prices over time?
x: At 3 percent inflation, something that costs $100 now would cost about $103 a year later.

q: Which stock exchange is located on Wall Street in New York City?
x: Wall Street got its name from a wall built by Dutch settlers in the 1600s.

q: Which Swedish company was founded by Ingvar Kamprad?
x: The name IKEA combines his initials with the first letters of his family farm, Elmtaryd, and village, Agunnaryd.

q: Which company was founded in 1998 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin?
x: The name is a play on 'googol', the number 1 followed by 100 zeros.

q: The yen is the official currency of which country?
x: The word yen means 'round object' in Japanese, and the currency has been in use since 1871.

q: Bitcoin was introduced in 2008 by a person or group using which pseudonym?
x: The real identity behind the name has never been confirmed.

q: Which animal is used as a symbol of a rising stock market?
x: A bull thrusts its horns upward while a bear swipes downward, which is the usual explanation for the terms.

q: What does LLC stand for in a company name?
x: The structure protects owners' personal assets from most business debts.

q: A balance sheet lists a company's assets, its liabilities, and what else?
x: The sheet always balances because assets equal liabilities plus equity.

q: Scurvy, once common among sailors on long voyages, is caused by a lack of which nutrient?
x: Scurvy once killed many sailors on long voyages until citrus fruit was added to their diet.

q: Which organ produces insulin?
x: Insulin was first used to treat diabetes in 1922.

q: What is the largest organ of the human body?
x: An adult's skin covers around 20 square feet and renews itself roughly every month.

q: What does BMI stand for?
x: It is calculated from weight and height and is only a rough screening tool.

q: Which blood type is considered the universal donor for red blood cells?
x: O negative red cells lack the markers that can trigger a reaction, so they are used in emergencies.

q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
x: It has two upper atria and two lower ventricles.

q: Which hormone, released in the dark, is nicknamed the sleep hormone?
x: Bright screens at night can reduce melatonin levels and make it harder to fall asleep.

q: Which colored part of the eye adjusts the size of the pupil?
x: Iris is Greek for 'rainbow', a nod to its range of colors.

q: Which ancient Greek physician is often called the father of medicine?
x: Doctors have traditionally taken an oath tied to his name, promising to act in the interest of patients.

q: Which planet in our solar system rotates on its side?
x: Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees, so its poles take turns pointing at the Sun during its 84-year orbit.

q: Which NASA mission carried the first humans to land on the Moon?
x: The crew was Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins, who stayed in lunar orbit.

q: Who became the first human in space in 1961?
x: His flight aboard Vostok 1 lasted 108 minutes and made one orbit of Earth.

q: Which space telescope, launched in 1990, is named after an American astronomer?
x: Its early images were blurry because of a flaw in its mirror, which astronauts fixed in 1993.

q: In which constellation is Polaris, the North Star, found?
x: Polaris sits at the end of the Little Dipper's handle and stays nearly fixed in the northern sky.

q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
x: The Sun is about 93 million miles away, and light covers it in roughly eight minutes and twenty seconds.

q: Which Renaissance artist painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
x: Michelangelo painted it between 1508 and 1512, mostly while standing, not lying on his back.

q: Which ancient Greek scholar is famous for shouting 'Eureka!' in a bathtub?
x: The story goes that he realized how to measure an object's volume by how much water it displaced.

q: Which Polish-born scientist won Nobel Prizes in both Physics and Chemistry?
x: She remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.

q: Who was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean?
x: She made the flight in May 1932 and received a Distinguished Flying Cross for it.

q: Which British mathematician helped break Germany's Enigma code in World War II?
x: His ideas laid the foundation for modern computer science, and the Turing Award is named after him.

q: Which English mathematician designed the Analytical Engine, a mechanical general-purpose computer, in the 1830s?
x: The machine was never fully built in his lifetime, but its design included a memory and a processor.

q: Who is often regarded as the world's first computer programmer?
x: In 1843 she published an algorithm intended for Babbage's Analytical Engine.

q: Which Italian physicist invented the first electric battery around 1800?
x: The unit of electric potential, the volt, is named in his honor.

q: A melted candy bar in an engineer's pocket in the 1940s led to the invention of which appliance?
x: Percy Spencer was testing radar equipment when he noticed the snack melting, and Raytheon soon sold the first microwave ovens.

q: Velcro was inspired by the seed pods of which plant?
x: Swiss engineer George de Mestral noticed burrs stuck to his dog's fur after a walk in the 1940s.

q: Who developed the first successful smallpox vaccine in 1796?
x: The word 'vaccine' comes from the Latin 'vacca', meaning cow, because Jenner used cowpox material.

q: Sticky notes were invented at which company?
x: Post-it Notes grew out of a weak adhesive discovered by Spencer Silver, with Art Fry finding a use for it as a bookmark.

q: Which Hungarian professor invented a famous twisting cube puzzle in 1974?
x: He originally built it as a teaching tool to help students understand three-dimensional movement.

q: Which Spanish architect designed the Sagrada Familia church in Barcelona?
x: Construction began in 1882, and the church is still being completed more than 140 years later.

q: In which Brazilian city does the Christ the Redeemer statue stand?
x: The statue stands 98 feet tall on top of Corcovado mountain and opened in 1931.

q: The glass pyramid entrance designed by I. M. Pei belongs to which Paris museum?
x: The pyramid opened in 1989 and was controversial at first because of its modern look beside the old palace.

q: Which bridge links San Francisco to Marin County across the bay's entrance?
x: Its color is officially called International Orange, and it was the longest suspension bridge in the world when it opened in 1937.

q: Which London bridge, opened in 1894, is often mistaken for London Bridge?
x: Its central sections lift so tall ships can pass through on the Thames.

q: The famous Leaning Tower stands in which Italian city?
x: It began to lean during construction in the 1100s because the soil beneath it was too soft.

q: Which civilization built the mountaintop city of Machu Picchu?
x: It was likely built in the 1400s as an estate for an Inca emperor and was unknown to the outside world until 1911.

q: In which country is the New Year's celebration called Hogmanay observed?
x: Traditions include 'first-footing', where the first visitor of the new year brings small gifts.

q: Cinco de Mayo commemorates a military victory in which country?
x: It marks the 1862 Battle of Puebla and is celebrated more widely in the US than in most of Mexico.

q: According to a popular superstition, breaking a mirror brings how many years of bad luck?
x: The belief goes back to the ancient Romans, who thought life renewed itself in seven-year cycles.

q: Which red flower is a symbol of remembrance in many Commonwealth countries each November?
x: The poppy became a symbol after wild poppies bloomed on battlefields in Europe after World War I.

q: International Women's Day is observed on which date?
x: The day has been marked since the early 1900s and is a public holiday in many countries.

q: What does SMS stand for?
x: The first text message was sent in December 1992.

q: What does URL stand for?
x: A URL tells your browser where to find a page and how to retrieve it.

q: What does QR stand for in QR code?
x: A Japanese company invented QR codes in 1994 to track car parts, and they were designed to be read quickly.

q: What does JPEG stand for?
x: It names the committee that created the image compression standard in the early 1990s.

q: Which company released the Walkman, its first portable cassette player, in 1979?
x: The first Walkman was a hit, helping change how people listened to music on the go.

q: What does the Latin phrase 'carpe diem' mean?
x: It comes from a poem by the Roman poet Horace written around 23 BC.

q: Which emergency phone number works across the entire European Union?
x: 112 also works from most mobile phones around the world, even without a SIM card in some regions.

q: The invitation abbreviation RSVP comes from a French phrase meaning what?
x: The full phrase is 'repondez s'il vous plait'.

q: How many items are in a baker's dozen?
x: The extra roll was originally added by bakers to avoid penalties for selling underweight bread.

q: Which wedding anniversary is traditionally associated with gold?
x: The 25th anniversary is silver, and the 60th is diamond.

q: In the phrase 'four score and seven years ago', how many years is a score?
x: Lincoln began the Gettysburg Address this way, meaning 87 years.

q: Which month is named in honor of Julius Caesar?
x: August was later named after the first Roman emperor, Augustus.

q: In 12-hour time, what does 'AM' stand for?
x: It is Latin for 'before midday', and PM means 'post meridiem', or 'after midday'.

q: Which number is considered especially lucky in Chinese culture because it sounds like 'prosperity'?
x: The 2008 Beijing Olympics opened on 8/8/08 at 8:08 p.m.

q: Which art movement is Claude Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise' associated with?
x: A critic mockingly used the painting's title to name the whole movement.

q: The word 'kindergarten', meaning 'children's garden', comes from which language?
x: Friedrich Froebel opened the first kindergarten in Germany in 1837.

q: What is a person who collects stamps called?
x: A numismatist collects coins, and a deltiologist collects postcards.

q: Which artist created the pop art works 'Campbell's Soup Cans'?
x: He first showed the 32 canvases in 1962, one for each soup flavor then sold.

q: Which Spanish artist painted the anti-war mural 'Guernica'?
x: The black, white, and gray painting is more than 25 feet wide.

q: Which Founding Father of the United States invented the lightning rod?
x: Franklin proposed it in the 1750s after studying electricity, and it protected buildings from fire.

q: Which businessman introduced the moving assembly line for cars in 1913?
x: The assembly line cut the time to build a Model T from over 12 hours to about 90 minutes.

q: What does the German word 'Volkswagen' mean in English?
x: The company was created in 1937 to build an affordable car for ordinary families.

q: Who created the Linux kernel in 1991?
x: He began it as a hobby project while a student in Finland; today Linux powers Android and most servers.

q: What is the name of the NASA rover that landed on Mars in 2021?
x: It carried a small helicopter, Ingenuity, which made the first powered flight on another planet.

q: How many moons does Mars have?
x: Phobos and Deimos are small and lumpy and may be captured asteroids.

q: Which comet returns to Earth's skies about every 76 years?
x: Edmond Halley correctly predicted its return after studying earlier sightings.

q: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
x: Arteries have thick, elastic walls to handle the pressure of each heartbeat.

q: What is the typical resting heart rate range for a healthy adult?
x: Very fit athletes can have a resting heart rate below 60.
